newsitem.title: TAIWAN: China approves Taiwan firms for historic sailings.
newsitem.headline: China approves Taiwan firms for historic sailings.

text.p: China on Thursday gave six Taiwan shipping firms approval to sail direct Taiwan-China routes for the first time in 48 years, reciprocating for similar permits issued by Taipei to five mainland shippers.

Executives said sailings could come as early as Friday, easing a ban enforced by Taipei since a 1949 civil war turned the narrow Taiwan strait into an ideological flash-point dividing China's Communists and Nationalists.
The private Taiwan Strait Shipping Association said it had received notice from its quasi-official mainland counterpart on Thursday that six Taiwan shipping firms had been approved.

Taiwan giants Uniglory Marine Corp and Yangming Marine Transport Corp confirmed that they had both been given a green light by Beijing. "They notified us today that we should pick up the licence," Uniglory vice president Wang Rong-hsiung told Reuters.
Eager to be first, Yangming said it could begin at a moment's notice with an auspiciously renamed container ship Gin Quan -- Golden Champion -- waiting at the southern port of Kaohsiung.

Taiwan media have said China's Sheng Da planned to sail from the mainland port of Xiamen as early as Thursday for arrival in Kaohsiung on Friday, though Kaohsiung officials said they had yet to receive mandatory 24-hour advance notice.

The rivals' reciprocal approvals eliminated the final hurdle to direct sailings, though Taipei -- wary of Beijing's political intentions -- has enacted restrictions forbidding direct cargo exchanges so as to uphold its ban on direct mainland links.
Mainland cargoes will not be allowed to enter Taiwan customs but can be processed at Kaohsiung's new "offshore transshipment centre" for onward passage to third countries.
Likewise, Taiwan cargoes at Kaohsiung cannot be put aboard ships planning to cross directly to the Chinese mainland.

Taipei has banned direct links since the Republic of China, defeated by the communists in 1949, fled into exile on Taiwan. Beijing sees Taiwan as a rebel-held province that eventually must be brought under its sovereignty.
A political thaw begun in the late 1980s has unleashed an explosion of indirect links, including some US$30 billion in mainland investments by 30,000 Taiwan firms.
Those investors have pressed Taipei to ease its ban, saying direct sea, air and other links would pare away what they see as needless extra costs of routing business through Hong Kong.
Consummation of direct shipping links comes when Taipei -- loath to become over-dependent on its rival's economy -- is trying to cool local firms' ardour for mainland investments.
Aside from Uniglory and Yangming, Beijing issued approvals to Taiwan's Wan Hai Lines, Nantai Line, Chinese Maritime Transport Ltd and Kien Hung Shipping.
The approvals came on what Taiwan experts said was the final possible day under mainland law mandating that Beijing act on such applications within 45 days of receiving them.
